newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Infotech pact seen giving symbolic boost to WTO.
newsitem.headline: Infotech pact seen giving symbolic boost to WTO.

text.p: A successful agreement this week on a plan to scrap tariffs on information technology will give the fledgling World Trade Organisation an important symbolic boost and reward months of hard diplomatic driving by the United States.

A broad deal that would cap the first meeting of WTO ministers was within reach on Thursday when the United States and the European Union (EU), after days of intense round-the-clock negotiations, settled differences over products to be included in an Information Technology Agreement (ITA).
"The basis of what we have agreed with the United States provides for a deal on ITA which will be a huge advance for the world economy," EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told a news conference.

The United States, backed by Japan, had been pushing for months for the agreement to eliminate tariffs by 2000. U.S. officials saw it as a way to give a boost to the two-year-old WTO as a trade liberalisation body.

"Here is an organisation that everybody thought couldn't do anything and they come up with a very important agreement," said Gary Horlick, a Washington trade attorney attending this week's WTO meeting in Singapore.

Details on the timing of tariff cuts were left to be worked out by negotiators in January. The EU's Brittan said the Europeans want an accelerated tariff reduction schedule, but the Asian countries who have expressed interest in joining the ITA want more flexibility on the timing of cuts.

The United States and European Union were pressing Thursday to bring as many countries as possible on board. The agreement is not to take effect unless about 90 percent of the $600 billion world trade in information technologies is covered.
The Big Four trade partners -- the United States, Canada, European Union and Japan -- account for about 55 percent of the global trade in information technology.
Up to 30 countries were said by officials to be interested in joining the ITA. EU and U.S. officials were keen to win support from as many Asian countries as possible.
"We have been working with the Asian countries for many months," said Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.

The success of the ITA at WTO was also important for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, U.S. officials said. APEC, after some high-level persuasion by President Bill Clinton, backed the ITA last month, creating momentum for an accord at this week's WTO ministerial conference, they said.

U.S. officials, who want to reduce the huge U.S. trade deficit and are anxious to see trade barriers fall around the globe, believe the ITA will give a boost to pending global trade negotiations to open up telephone and financial service markets.
Trade analysts have also said it will give the Clinton administration something to show wary members of the U.S. Congress -- that trade agreements benefit workers and consumers.

The White House faces a tough fight next year to win congressional approval of legislation that would allow the administration to negotiate an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) to include Chile. NAFTA groups Canada, the United States and Mexico in a free trade zone.

Horlick praised Barshefsky, who would like to seek the "acting" removed from her title, for her efforts to win an ITA accord. Barshefsky has been serving as acting U.S. trade representative since Mickey Kantor left the post to become commerce secretary earlier this year.
"They should make her USTR," Horlick said.
